events.title: Grapevines domesticated in two places at once
events.text: A 2023 study in Science, led by Yang Dong and Wei Chen with 89 co-authors, sequenced 3,525 wild and cultivated grapevines and concluded that grapes were domesticated about 11,000 years ago in two places at the same time: the South Caucasus, for wine, and western Asia (the Levant and Anatolia), for table grapes. Farmers took the western Asian table grapes into Europe, where they crossed with local wild vines, producing the ancestors of today's Western European wine grapes. The two-centre model overturned the older idea of a single wine domestication in the Caucasus.

sources.title: Dong et al. 2023, Science: Dual domestications and origin of traits in grapevine evolution
CIRAD: Domestication of the grapevine revisited

events.title: Jiahu: the oldest known fermented drink
events.text: Pottery jars from Jiahu, a Neolithic village in Henan province, China, held residues of a mixed fermented drink made from rice, honey and fruit, probably hawthorn and wild grape. Patrick McGovern and colleagues published the chemical analysis in 2004, dating the drink to around 7000 to 6600 BC, the oldest chemically attested alcoholic beverage. It was not grape wine as we know it: China's wild grapes were never domesticated for wine. But it shows that people across Eurasia were fermenting fruit and grain long before vineyards existed.

sources.title: Penn Museum: Patrick McGovern biomolecular archaeology

events.title: Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora: the first grape wine
events.text: At two Neolithic villages of the Shulaveri-Shomu culture, about 50 km south of Tbilisi, archaeologists found pottery jars with tartaric acid and other grape markers. Published in PNAS in November 2017 by Patrick McGovern, Stephen Batiuk, Mindia Jalabadze and colleagues, the finds date to about 6000 BC, the earliest chemical evidence of wine made from grapes. Some jars were decorated with grape clusters. Georgia uses the discovery to support its claim to be the 'cradle of wine', and the find fits the 2023 genetic evidence of early domestication in the South Caucasus.

sources.title: Sci.News: Ancient Georgian pottery reveals world's oldest wine (2017)

events.title: Hajji Firuz Tepe: wine sealed with resin
events.text: In a mud-brick house in the Zagros mountains of northwestern Iran, six clay jars of about nine litres each stood set into the kitchen floor. In 1996 Patrick McGovern's team detected tartaric acid and terebinth tree resin, added as a preservative, in a yellowish residue. For two decades this was the oldest chemical evidence of grape wine. The resin shows that early winemakers already knew wine spoiled and that additives could protect it, a practice that survives in Greek retsina.
events.place: Hajji Firuz Tepe, West Azerbaijan, Iran

events.title: Areni-1: the oldest known winery
events.text: In a cave above the Arpa river in Armenia, archaeologists led by Boris Gasparyan and Gregory Areshian uncovered a shallow clay treading floor sloping into a large jar, with grape seeds, pressed skins and drinking cups around it. Published in January 2011 and dated to about 4100 BC, it is the oldest known winery, built for production rather than household use. The cave also held burials, suggesting wine was used in rituals for the dead. The neighbouring village gives its name to Armenia's leading red grape, Areni.

events.title: Godin Tepe: wine in a Mesopotamian trade post
events.text: At Godin Tepe, a fortified trading post on the Great Khorasan Road in western Iran, jars with red stains and tartaric acid residues were found lying on their sides, with holes near the base, suggesting wine was stored with its sediment and decanted. Dated to about 3500 to 3100 BC, the find shows wine moving along trade routes connecting the Zagros highlands with the cities of Sumer, where wine was a rare luxury imported from the mountains while beer was the everyday drink.

events.title: Scorpion I's tomb: 700 jars of imported wine
events.text: Tomb U-j at Abydos, built for a ruler of Upper Egypt known as Scorpion I, contained about 700 wine jars of roughly 6 litres each, stacked four rows deep in three chambers. Chemical analysis showed resinated grape wine, and clay analysis showed the jars were made in the southern Levant, so the wine had been imported. Some jars held sliced figs, perhaps to sweeten or start fermentation. The find shows how early wine was tied to kingship, and it prompted the Egyptians to plant their own royal vineyards in the Nile Delta.

events.title: Hammurabi's code regulates the wine shop
events.text: The law code of Hammurabi of Babylon, carved on a basalt stele, includes rules for tavern keepers, who were usually women selling beer and date wine. Overcharging was punished by drowning, and a priestess who opened or entered a tavern could be burned. Grape wine was an expensive import from the northern mountains, but the code shows that alcohol sales were already subject to state control and price rules, an ancestor of the licensing and taxation that would follow wine through history.

events.title: Santorini's buried vineyards
events.text: The Bronze Age town of Akrotiri on Santorini was buried by a massive volcanic eruption around 1600 BC, preserving storage jars, presses and frescoes. The ash and pumice later became the soil of Santorini's vineyards, which phylloxera could never colonise. Island growers still train Assyrtiko into low baskets, the kouloura, to protect it from wind. Santorini's vineyards are among the oldest continuously cultivated in Europe.

events.title: Tutankhamun's labelled vintages
events.text: Among the treasures in Tutankhamun's tomb in the Valley of the Kings were 26 wine jars with inscriptions recording the vintage year of his reign, the estate, the owner and the chief vintner, such as 'Year 5, sweet wine of the house of Aten, chief vintner Aperershop'. It is the earliest known wine labelling. Most came from vineyards in the western Nile Delta. Later analysis found that some held red wine and one a white wine (shedeh), showing Egyptians made both.

events.title: The Uluburun wreck and Bronze Age wine trade
events.text: Off the Turkish coast near Kaş, divers in the 1980s excavated a ship that sank around 1300 BC carrying copper and tin ingots, glass, ivory and Canaanite jars, some holding terebinth resin and others grape pips. Its cargo, from Cyprus, the Levant, Egypt and Mycenaean Greece, shows how wine travelled in the Bronze Age Mediterranean, in amphora-like jars traded among palace economies. Linear B tablets from Pylos and Knossos from the same era record vineyards and wine rations.

events.title: Nuragic Sardinia and early western wine
events.text: Grape seeds found at Nuragic sites in Sardinia, such as Sa Osa near Cabras (dated to the late Bronze Age), and stone basins interpreted as presses have been offered as evidence that Sardinians made wine before Phoenician contact. Some Sardinian scholars use them to argue that Cannonau (Grenache) originated on the island. The claims are debated, but they show that western Mediterranean winemaking may be older than once believed.

events.title: Phoenicians carry the vine west
events.text: Traders from Tyre, Sidon and Byblos spread wine and viticulture across the Mediterranean, founding colonies at Carthage (traditionally 814 BC), Gadir (Cádiz) and Sardinia. Their amphorae and the vines they planted helped bring winemaking to North Africa, southern Spain and the islands. Mago of Carthage later wrote a 28-volume agricultural manual, translated into Latin by order of the Roman Senate after Carthage fell in 146 BC, that influenced Roman vineyard practice.

events.title: Greeks found Massalia
events.text: Greek colonists from Phocaea in Asia Minor founded Massalia (Marseille) around 600 BC. They planted vines and traded wine up the Rhône with the Celts, who paid high prices: a Celtic chief would swap a slave for an amphora, according to Diodorus Siculus. Massaliote amphorae turn up across southern France, and the colony laid the foundations of Provençal and Rhône viticulture. Excavations at Lattara near Montpellier found a wine press dated to about 425 BC, the oldest in France.

events.title: The Greek symposium
events.text: In Athens and across the Greek world, the symposium was an all-male drinking party where wine was mixed with water in a large krater, usually three parts water to one of wine, and served by the cup under the direction of a symposiarch. Drinking unmixed wine was considered barbaric. Plato's Symposium (c. 385 BC) is set at one. Painted pottery, songs, games such as kottabos and philosophical debate grew around it, making wine the centre of Greek social and intellectual life.

events.title: Thasos: the first wine-quality laws
events.text: Inscriptions from the island of Thasos in the northern Aegean record some of the earliest known wine regulations. They banned the sale of wine by the jug before the first month of autumn, forbade local boats from importing foreign wine into the island's coast, and regulated sales. Thasian wine was famous and exported in stamped amphorae across the Black Sea and Mediterranean. The laws protected the wine's reputation and the island's trade, an early version of the logic behind appellation rules.

events.title: Roman writers create vineyard science
events.text: Cato the Elder's De Agri Cultura (c. 160 BC) described how to run a vineyard with slave labour; Varro, Columella (De Re Rustica, c. AD 60) and Pliny the Elder's Natural History (AD 77) went much further, discussing grape varieties, soils, trellising, pruning, yields and winemaking. Columella argued that vineyards were the most profitable farming and advised on planting density and pruning that remain recognisable. These texts were copied by medieval monks and shaped European viticulture for 1,500 years.

events.title: Zhang Qian brings vines to Han China
events.text: The Han envoy Zhang Qian returned from Central Asia with reports of grape wine in Dayuan (Ferghana), where wealthy households stored large quantities for years. Soon afterwards vinifera grapes and alfalfa were planted near the imperial palaces at Chang'an. Grape wine never displaced grain alcohol in China, but it remained an exotic luxury, especially under the Tang dynasty, when wine from the Turpan oasis was presented to the emperor.

events.title: The Opimian vintage
events.text: The year of the consul Lucius Opimius produced a legendary Roman vintage, remembered for generations. Pliny the Elder wrote that Opimian wine still existed nearly 200 years later, reduced to a bitter, honey-like syrup that was used to flavour other wines. Its fame shows that Romans valued old wine and tracked vintages by consul. Falernian from the Ager Falernus on the slopes of Monte Massico in Campania was the most prized wine of the time, graded into dry and sweet styles and different crus.

events.title: Carmona: the oldest liquid wine
events.text: In 2019 builders in Carmona near Seville uncovered an intact Roman family tomb. One glass urn held cremated bones, a gold ring and about five litres of reddish liquid. A team led by José Rafael Ruiz Arrebola and Daniel Cosano of the University of Córdoba analysed it and in June 2024 published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports that it was a white wine, about 2,000 years old, similar to sherry-style wines of the region. It displaced the Speyer bottle as the oldest wine preserved in liquid form.

sources.title: Scientific American: Oldest wine in the world is a 2,000-year-old white from Spain

events.title: Vesuvius buries Pompeii's vineyards
events.text: In late AD 79 (traditionally 24 August, though recent finds suggest October), Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii, a busy wine town whose amphorae were exported across the empire. Excavations revealed scores of street bars (thermopolia), wine shops, presses and vineyards inside the city walls, where archaeologists cast the cavities left by ancient roots. Since the 1990s the Mastroberardino family has replanted vines on excavated plots with ancient Campanian varieties. Pliny the Elder died in the eruption.

events.title: Domitian's vine edict
events.text: Faced with a grain shortage and a wine glut, Emperor Domitian ordered that no new vines be planted in Italy and that half the vineyards in the provinces be uprooted, according to Suetonius. The edict was probably meant to protect Italian wine producers and encourage grain growing. It was poorly enforced, but it is often cited as the first attempt at a European vineyard planting policy, a theme that returned in EU planting rights and grubbing-up schemes 1,900 years later.

events.title: Probus lifts the ban and plants the Rhine and Danube
events.text: Emperor Probus, born in Sirmium in Pannonia, revoked Domitian's restrictions and, according to the Historia Augusta, allowed all Gauls, Spaniards and Britons to plant vines. He is said to have set soldiers to planting vineyards on the Danube and in Pannonia. Roman vineyards were already spreading along the Mosel and Rhine, where the Neumagen wine ship relief (c. 220) shows barrels being carried by boat, but Probus became the legendary patron of northern European winemaking.

events.title: The Speyer bottle
events.text: A sealed glass bottle with a layer of olive oil over the wine was buried with a Roman nobleman near Speyer in the Rhineland. Found in 1867, it was long the oldest unopened bottle of wine, now displayed in the Historical Museum of the Palatinate. It shows that wine was part of Roman funerary ritual and that vines had spread to the Rhine. In 2024 a liquid Roman wine from Carmona in Spain, about 300 years older, took its title.

events.title: Ausonius praises the Mosel
events.text: Decimus Magnus Ausonius, a poet from Bordeaux serving at the imperial court in Trier, wrote the Mosella, a long Latin poem describing vineyards rising up the steep slopes of the Mosel, their reflections in the river and the songs of vine-dressers. It is the first literary portrait of the valley's slate vineyards. Ausonius also owned estates near Bordeaux, and Château Ausone in Saint-Émilion takes its name from him.
events.place: Trier and the Mosel valley, Germany

events.title: Monks keep the vineyards alive
events.text: Benedict of Nursia founded Monte Cassino in 529, and his Rule allowed monks a measured daily ration of wine. As the Western Roman Empire collapsed, monasteries and bishops kept vineyards going for the Eucharist, hospitality and income. Benedictine abbeys, and later Cistercian ones, became Europe's leading viticulturists, recording yields and selecting sites, from Burgundy to the Rhine. Charlemagne's Capitulare de villis (c. 800) required clean presses and careful winemaking on royal estates.

events.title: Abu Nuwas and the wine poetry of Baghdad
events.text: Although the Quran forbids intoxicating drink, wine remained part of court culture in Abbasid Baghdad, much of it made by Christian and Jewish vintners. Abu Nuwas (c. 756 to 814), the city's most celebrated poet, wrote khamriyyat, wine poems praising taverns and old vintages. Centuries later, Persian poets such as Hafez of Shiraz used wine as both a real pleasure and a mystical symbol. Vines survived in Islamic lands for table grapes and raisins, and some Muslim scholars refined distillation.

events.title: The Norse name 'Vinland'
events.text: According to the Icelandic sagas, Leif Erikson sailed west from Greenland around 1000 and named a land 'Vinland' after the wild grapes his crew found. The Norse settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, excavated in the 1960s, confirmed that Vikings reached North America. Butternuts found there grow only further south, suggesting they explored regions where wild grapes such as Vitis riparia grow. The name became an early record of North America's wild vines.

events.title: Cistercians build the Clos de Vougeot
events.text: Monks from Cîteaux Abbey, founded in 1098, received their first vineyard parcels at Vougeot in the early 12th century and gradually assembled about 50 hectares, enclosed by a stone wall by 1336. The Cistercians observed how wines from different plots tasted different, laying the foundations of the Burgundian idea of the climat. Their château, cellars and presses at Vougeot still stand. Cistercians also founded Kloster Eberbach in the Rheingau in 1136, Germany's leading medieval wine estate.

events.title: Eleanor of Aquitaine marries Henry Plantagenet
events.text: When Eleanor of Aquitaine married Henry, Count of Anjou, in 1152 and he became Henry II of England two years later, Bordeaux and Gascony came under the English crown for three centuries. English demand for light red 'clairet' from Bordeaux created a huge export trade: in peak years of the early 14th century the port shipped tens of thousands of tonneaux. The English word claret dates from this relationship. The link ended with the French victory at Castillon in 1453.

events.title: Commandaria and the Knights of Cyprus
events.text: After Richard the Lionheart took Cyprus in 1191, the island passed to the Templars and then the Knights Hospitaller, whose Grand Commandery at Kolossi near Limassol gave its name to a sweet wine made from sun-dried Mavro and Xynisteri grapes. Commandaria was exported across medieval Europe, and Cyprus claims it as the oldest named wine still made. Today it is produced in 14 villages on the southern slopes of the Troodos mountains, under a protected designation.

events.title: The popes move to Avignon
events.text: When Clement V moved the papal court to Avignon in 1309, the region's vineyards gained powerful patrons. His successor John XXII built a summer residence at Châteauneuf, the 'new castle of the pope', and promoted the local vineyards. The court also bought heavily from Burgundy, raising Beaune's prestige. Much later, the name Châteauneuf-du-Pape and its papal keys would become a brand. The popes returned to Rome in 1377.

events.title: Philip the Bold bans the 'disloyal Gamay'
events.text: Duke Philip the Bold of Burgundy ordered growers to uproot Gamay, which he called 'a very bad and disloyal plant', and to stop fertilising vineyards with manure, which raised yields at the expense of quality. The decree protected the reputation of Burgundy's Pinot-based wines, which the duke used as diplomatic gifts. It is one of the earliest European laws on grape variety and quality. Gamay retreated south to Beaujolais.

events.title: First record of Riesling
events.text: An inventory of the cellars of Count John IV of Katzenelnbogen at Rüsselsheim on the Main records a purchase of 'seczlinge riesslingen in die wingarten', Riesling cuttings for the vineyard, for 22 shillings. It is the oldest known written reference to the grape. Over the next three centuries Riesling spread along the Rhine and Mosel, encouraged by later decrees such as those of the Archbishop of Trier (1787) favouring it over lesser varieties.

events.title: The Hospices de Beaune is founded
events.text: Nicolas Rolin, chancellor to the Duke of Burgundy, and his wife Guigone de Salins founded the Hôtel-Dieu in Beaune as a hospital for the poor. Over the centuries benefactors donated vineyards, and since 1859 the Hospices has sold its wines at a charity auction each November, long run by Christie's and since 2021 by Sotheby's. The results are watched as a barometer of Burgundy prices. The estate holds about 60 hectares, much of it premier and grand cru.

events.title: Castillon ends English Bordeaux
events.text: French forces defeated the English at Castillon on the Dordogne, ending the Hundred Years' War and three centuries of English rule in Gascony. Bordeaux lost its privileged access to England, and for a time Dutch merchants became the dominant buyers of Bordeaux and Loire wines. The Dutch later drained the Médoc marshes in the 17th century, opening the gravel ridges on which the great châteaux would be founded.

events.title: Cortés orders vines planted in New Spain
events.text: Hernán Cortés decreed in 1524 that every Spanish settler in Mexico with Indigenous labourers must plant ten vines a year per hundred workers. The Listán Prieto grape (later called Mission, País and Criolla Chica) spread with the conquest: to Peru by the 1540s, Chile by the 1550s and Argentina by the 1550s. Spain later restricted colonial wine to protect its own exports, but Casa Madero at Parras, founded in 1597, survives as the oldest winery in the Americas.
events.place: Parras de la Fuente, Coahuila, Mexico

events.title: The siege of Eger and 'Bull's Blood'
events.text: In 1552 a small Hungarian garrison under István Dobó held the castle of Eger against a much larger Ottoman army. Legend says the defenders drank red wine before battle, and the Turks, seeing their red-stained beards, thought they were drinking bull's blood and lost heart. The story gave the name Egri Bikavér (Bull's Blood of Eger), a red blend now based on Kékfrankos. Eger's wine cellars, carved into the soft volcanic tuff of the Valley of the Beautiful Women, are a local landmark.

events.title: Tokaji Aszú is born
events.text: Wines made from shrivelled, botrytised (aszú) grapes are recorded in Tokaj from at least 1571, and a 1576 dictionary by Balázs Fabricius Sziksai mentions them. Legend credits the Calvinist preacher Máté Szepsi Laczkó with the first aszú in about 1630, when a harvest delayed by Turkish raids left grapes to rot. In 1631 the Tokaj towns adopted rules for aszú production. The wine became a favourite of European courts: Louis XIV is said to have called it 'the wine of kings, the king of wines'.

events.title: Drake seizes 2,900 butts of sherry
events.text: In April 1587 Sir Francis Drake raided Cádiz, destroying Spanish ships and carrying off about 2,900 butts of 'sack', the fortified wine of Jerez. Sherry became fashionable in England: Shakespeare's Falstaff praises 'sherris-sack' in Henry IV, Part 2. English and Dutch merchants built a lasting trade, and in the 18th and 19th centuries British families founded many Jerez bodegas, including Harvey's, Osborne and Sandeman.

sources.title: Singeing the King of Spain's Beard

events.title: The first record of pisco
events.text: The will of Pedro Manuel, a Greek-born resident of Ica in Peru, dated 1613, lists a still and jars of grape spirit, the earliest known record of pisco. Spanish restrictions on colonial wine exports encouraged distilling, and the coastal valleys of Ica, Pisco and Moquegua became centres of brandy production for the silver mines of Potosí. Peru and Chile still dispute the name pisco; both protect it as a designation of origin.

events.title: Virginia's first wine law
events.text: The first assembly of the Virginia colony at Jamestown passed Acte 12, requiring every householder to plant ten vines and learn the art of vine dressing. French vignerons were brought in. The attempts failed: native diseases, phylloxera and Pierce's disease killed European vines, and tobacco was more profitable. For two centuries American viticulture struggled until native and hybrid grapes such as Norton and Catawba offered a way forward.

events.title: First wine in the Cape
events.text: Jan van Riebeeck, commander of the Dutch East India Company's Cape station, wrote in his diary on 2 February 1659: 'Today, praise be to God, wine was pressed for the first time from Cape grapes.' Vines had been planted in 1655 to help prevent scurvy among sailors. In 1685 Governor Simon van der Stel founded Constantia, and from 1688 French Huguenot refugees brought winemaking skills to Franschhoek.

events.title: Christopher Merret describes sparkling wine
events.text: The English physician and scientist Christopher Merret presented a paper to the Royal Society describing how coopers and wine merchants added 'great quantities of sugar and molasses' to wine to make it 'drink brisk and sparkling'. It is the earliest documented account of deliberately making wine sparkle by a second fermentation. English glassmakers were already producing bottles strong enough, thanks to coal-fired furnaces. The paper predates Dom Pérignon's work at Hautvillers, which aimed to prevent bubbles.

events.title: Pepys drinks 'Ho Bryan'
events.text: Samuel Pepys wrote in his diary that at the Royal Oak tavern in London he drank 'a sort of French wine called Ho Bryan, that hath a good and most particular taste that I never met with'. It is the first written reference to a wine identified by its estate, Château Haut-Brion in Graves. The Pontac family, owners since 1525, pioneered selling wine under a property name and later opened a fashionable London tavern, the Pontack's Head, in 1666.

events.title: Dom Pérignon at Hautvillers
events.text: The Benedictine monk Pierre Pérignon became cellarer of the Abbey of Hautvillers above Épernay in 1668 and held the post until his death in 1715. He did not invent sparkling Champagne; he worked to improve still wines, blending grapes from different vineyards, pressing black grapes gently to make white wine and reducing unwanted refermentation. His reputation, embellished by later monks, became central to Champagne's mythology, and Moët & Chandon named its prestige cuvée after him in 1936.

events.title: The Methuen Treaty
events.text: England and Portugal signed a commercial treaty negotiated by John Methuen: Portugal admitted English woollens, and England promised that Portuguese wines would never pay more than two thirds of the duty on French wines. During wars with France, English merchants in Porto shipped growing quantities of Douro wine, adding brandy to stabilise it for the voyage. The treaty helped create Port and tied the Douro's economy to Britain for two centuries.

events.title: The Great Frost
events.text: The coldest European winter in 500 years killed vines across France: temperatures fell to around minus 20 degrees Celsius in Paris, and even the Atlantic coast froze. Vineyards around Nantes were replanted with the hardy Burgundian Melon, which became Muscadet. Many Bordeaux and Burgundy vineyards had to be replanted. The disaster raised prices and, by destroying old plantings, encouraged changes in grape varieties across France.

events.title: Cosimo III delimits Chianti
events.text: Grand Duke Cosimo III de' Medici issued a decree defining the borders of four wine zones: Chianti, Pomino, Carmignano and Val d'Arno di Sopra, and set up a body to oversee production and fight fraud. It is often called the first legal delimitation of a wine region. The Chianti zone covered the hills between Florence and Siena, roughly today's Chianti Classico. The decree came 140 years before Bettino Ricasoli's formula for the Chianti blend.

events.title: Tokaj's royal decree
events.text: A decree of King Charles III of Hungary (Emperor Charles VI) defined the boundaries of the Tokaj wine region, listing the villages entitled to produce Tokaji. Earlier, from 1730, the vineyards had been classified into first, second and third class growths, a ranking that predated Bordeaux's 1855 classification by more than a century. Tokaj's closed region and classified vineyards make it a strong candidate for the first appellation system in the world.

events.title: Pombal demarcates the Douro
events.text: After Port prices collapsed through overproduction and adulteration, Portugal's chief minister, the Marquis of Pombal, created the Companhia Geral da Agricultura das Vinhas do Alto Douro. It delimited the vineyards entitled to produce Port, marking them with granite posts (marcos pombalinos), classified vineyards by quality and controlled trade. Many of the original stones survive in the vineyards. The Douro is often called the world's first demarcated and regulated wine region.

sources.title: Companhia Geral da Agricultura das Vinhas do Alto Douro

events.title: The late courier of Schloss Johannisberg
events.text: Every year the monks of Schloss Johannisberg in the Rheingau had to wait for permission from their owner, the Prince-Abbot of Fulda, to begin the harvest. In 1775 the courier carrying the order was delayed for weeks. By the time he arrived, the grapes were shrivelled and rotten, but the wine made from them was extraordinary. The estate thus 'discovered' the value of late harvesting and noble rot: Spätlese. A statue of the courier stands in the courtyard.

events.title: Mission vines in Alta California
events.text: Franciscan friars led by Junípero Serra founded a chain of missions in Alta California from 1769, and Mission San Juan Capistrano is often credited with the first wine made in California, around 1779 to 1782, from the Mission grape (Listán Prieto). The missions made wine for Mass and for sale. Jean-Louis Vignes, a Frenchman from Bordeaux, imported European vines to Los Angeles in the 1830s, and the Gold Rush of 1849 created California's first commercial wine boom.

events.title: Vin de Constance, Napoleon's exile wine
events.text: Hendrik Cloete bought Groot Constantia in 1778 and made sweet wine from late-picked Muscat de Frontignan grapes that became one of the most sought-after wines in Europe, drunk by Frederick the Great and Louis-Philippe and mentioned by Jane Austen and Charles Dickens. Napoleon had it shipped to him in exile on Saint Helena. Oidium, phylloxera and the loss of preferential British tariffs destroyed the trade in the 19th century; Klein Constantia revived the style as Vin de Constance in 1986.
events.place: Groot Constantia, Cape Town, South Africa

events.title: Jefferson's tour of French vineyards
events.text: As American minister to France, Thomas Jefferson toured Burgundy, the Rhône, Bordeaux and the Rhine in 1787 and 1788, recording vineyard rankings and buying wine for himself and George Washington. His notes listed Bordeaux's four top growths (Margaux, La Tour de Ségur, Haut-Brion and Lafite), anticipating the 1855 ranking. He tried and failed to grow European vines at Monticello. In 1985 a bottle of 1787 Lafite engraved 'Th.J.' sold at Christie's for 105,000 pounds; the authenticity of these 'Jefferson bottles' was later challenged in court.

events.title: Veuve Clicquot invents the riddling table
events.text: Barbe-Nicole Ponsardin, widowed at 27 in 1805, took over her husband's Champagne house in Reims. Sediment from the second fermentation made sparkling wine cloudy, so in 1816 she and her cellar master Antoine de Müller developed the pupitre, a table with angled holes in which bottles were turned and tilted daily until the yeast collected in the neck. Riddling (remuage) made clear sparkling wine possible on a commercial scale and remained standard until gyropalettes arrived in the 1970s.

events.title: James Busby's vine collection
events.text: James Busby, a Scottish-born viticulturist who had taught in New South Wales, toured French and Spanish vineyards in 1831 and collected cuttings of about 650 varieties, which arrived in Sydney in 1832. Planted at the Botanic Gardens and at Busby's Hunter Valley property, Kirkton, the collection supplied many of Australia's earliest vineyards, including Syrah, which became Shiraz. Busby moved to New Zealand in 1833 as British Resident and planted vines at Waitangi, where he helped draft the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi.

events.title: Silesian Lutherans settle the Barossa
events.text: Lutheran refugees from Prussia and Silesia, fleeing religious persecution and backed by George Fife Angas, settled the Barossa Valley north of Adelaide from 1842 and planted vines. Their descendants founded wineries such as Seppelt (1851) and Henschke (1868), and the region became Australia's most famous for Shiraz. Because South Australia kept phylloxera out, the Barossa retains some of the world's oldest vines, including Shiraz and Grenache planted in the 1840s to 1880s.

events.title: Longworth's sparkling Catawba
events.text: Nicholas Longworth, a Cincinnati lawyer and land speculator, began making sparkling wine from the native Catawba grape on the slopes of the Ohio River around 1842. It was widely praised and inspired Longfellow's 'Ode to Catawba Wine' (1854). By the late 1850s Ohio was the leading wine-producing state in the US. Black rot and powdery mildew then destroyed the vineyards, and the industry moved to the shores of Lake Erie and to Missouri.

events.title: Penfolds is founded at Magill
events.text: Dr Christopher Rawson Penfold, an English doctor, and his wife Mary planted vines at Magill, at the foot of the Adelaide Hills, in 1844, intending to make fortified wines as tonics for anaemic patients. Mary Penfold ran the winery after his death in 1870. Penfolds grew into Australia's most famous producer, and Magill Estate, now within suburban Adelaide, became the birthplace of Grange a century later.

events.title: Powdery mildew sweeps Europe
events.text: In 1845 a gardener named Edward Tucker in Margate, Kent, noticed a white powder on greenhouse vines: oidium (powdery mildew, Erysiphe necator), a North American fungus. It reached France by 1847, and in the early 1850s it devastated vineyards across Europe, cutting French production by roughly three quarters within a few years. Madeira's vineyards were almost destroyed in 1852. Growers discovered that dusting vines with sulphur controlled it, a treatment still used, including in organic farming.

events.title: Ochagavía brings French vines to Chile
events.text: Silvestre Ochagavía Errázuriz hired French winemakers and imported cuttings of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Malbec, Sauvignon Blanc and others to the Maipo Valley in 1851, launching Chile's fine-wine industry. Because these vines arrived before phylloxera reached Europe, Chile's ungrafted vineyards preserved pre-phylloxera Bordeaux material, including Carmenère mixed in with Merlot. Chile has never been affected by phylloxera, thanks to its isolation between the Andes, the Pacific and the Atacama desert.

events.title: Madeira's double disaster
events.text: Madeira's wine trade had boomed in the 18th century, especially with the American colonies, which used it to toast the Declaration of Independence in 1776. In 1852 oidium destroyed most of the island's vineyards, and phylloxera followed in 1872. Many growers switched to sugar cane or American hybrids, and the noble grapes Sercial, Verdelho, Bual and Malmsey became rare, replaced largely by Tinta Negra. Madeira's estufagem and canteiro ageing traditions survived and its finest wines can live for two centuries.

events.title: Pouget brings Malbec to Mendoza
events.text: Domingo Faustino Sarmiento, later president of Argentina, hired the French agronomist Michel Aimé Pouget to run a new agricultural school in Mendoza. Pouget brought French vine cuttings, including Malbec, and the provincial law founding the Quinta Normal was approved on 17 April 1853. Italian and Spanish immigrants and the railway (1885) made Mendoza a mass producer. Argentina now celebrates World Malbec Day on 17 April.

events.title: The 1855 Bordeaux classification
events.text: For the Exposition Universelle in Paris, Napoleon III asked for a ranking of Bordeaux's best wines. The Bordeaux brokers' syndicate produced it in two weeks, based on decades of trading prices: 58 red wines from the Médoc plus Haut-Brion in five growths (crus), and 21 sweet wines of Sauternes and Barsac, with Château d'Yquem alone as Premier Cru Supérieur. It has been changed only twice: Cantemerle was added in September 1855, and Mouton Rothschild was promoted to first growth in 1973.

events.title: Haraszthy founds Buena Vista and collects European vines
events.text: Agoston Haraszthy, a Hungarian émigré, founded Buena Vista Winery in Sonoma in 1857, now California's oldest commercial winery. In 1861 he toured Europe on behalf of the state and returned with tens of thousands of cuttings of some 350 varieties. He promoted dry-farming on hillsides and is often called the father of California viticulture, though the extent of his role in introducing Zinfandel is disputed. He disappeared in Nicaragua in 1869, reputedly taken by an alligator.

events.title: Jesuits found Château Ksara
events.text: Jesuit priests founded Ksara in the Bekaa Valley in 1857, later planting Cinsault and other varieties from French Algeria, and began making dry red wine. The Jesuits discovered Roman-era caves nearby, which became the winery's cellars. Lebanon's wine tradition, traced back to the Phoenicians, revived under French influence. In 1930 Gaston Hochar founded Château Musar, which his son Serge made famous in the 1970s and 1980s by making wine through the civil war.

events.title: Pasteur explains fermentation and spoilage
events.text: Asked by Napoleon III to investigate why French wines spoiled, Louis Pasteur studied wine in his native Arbois in the Jura and showed that fermentation was the work of living yeasts and that spoilage came from other microorganisms. His 'Études sur le vin' (1866) recommended heating wine briefly to about 55 degrees Celsius to kill bacteria, a process later called pasteurisation. His work made modern oenology possible and moved winemaking from tradition toward science.

events.title: Phylloxera arrives in France
events.text: In 1863 vines began to die mysteriously in the Gard near Pujaut and Roquemaure, close to the Rhône. In July 1868 the botanist Jules-Émile Planchon and colleagues dug up dying vines at Saint-Martin-de-Crau and found the roots covered with a tiny yellow aphid, which he named Phylloxera vastatrix. It had arrived from North America on vines imported for collections, surviving the faster steamship voyages. Over the next three decades it destroyed most of the vineyards of France and then Europe.

events.title: Phylloxera reaches the Douro
events.text: Portugal's Douro was one of the first regions outside France to be hit: sources date the first infestations between 1865 and 1872. Within two decades much of the Port vineyard was dead, and the abandoned, collapsed terraces, the mortórios, can still be seen on the hillsides. Replanting on American rootstocks shifted vineyards to new sites, and the crisis encouraged Port shippers to buy their own quintas. Producers such as Quinta do Noval preserved a small plot of ungrafted vines, the source of the rare Nacional.

events.title: Concord grapes and Welch's juice
events.text: Ephraim Bull selected the Concord grape in Massachusetts in 1849. In 1869 Thomas Welch, a dentist and Methodist communion steward in Vineland, New Jersey, pasteurised Concord juice to create an unfermented 'sacramental wine' for the temperance movement. Welch's grape juice became a global brand, and Concord remains a staple of the Lake Erie and Finger Lakes regions. The story shows how temperance and native grapes shaped American viticulture.

events.title: Riley confirms the American origin
events.text: Charles Valentine Riley, Missouri's state entomologist, showed that the leaf-galling insect on American vines was the same as the root-feeding aphid killing French vineyards, and that American vines tolerated it. In 1871 he visited France and worked with Planchon. Their conclusion pointed to the solution: graft European vines onto American roots. France awarded Riley the Legion of Honour, and Montpellier later raised a statue honouring the American contribution.

events.title: French merchants transform Rioja
events.text: With phylloxera destroying French vineyards, Bordeaux merchants crossed the Pyrenees to buy wine in Rioja, bringing barrel ageing and new methods. Marqués de Riscal (founded 1858 in Elciego) and Marqués de Murrieta (first exports 1852) had already introduced Bordeaux techniques; the railway station at Haro became the centre of a cluster of new bodegas, including López de Heredia (1877), CVNE (1879) and La Rioja Alta (1890). The boom ended when phylloxera reached Rioja in 1901.

events.title: Harriague plants Tannat in Uruguay
events.text: Pascual Harriague, a Basque immigrant from France, planted Tannat near Salto in northwestern Uruguay around 1870. The variety thrived in Uruguay's humid Atlantic climate and became so associated with him that it was long called Harriague. Francisco Vidiella introduced other European varieties near Montevideo at the same time. Tannat is now Uruguay's national grape, and the country has the highest per capita wine consumption in South America.

events.title: Phylloxera arrives in Austria
events.text: Phylloxera was first found in Austria-Hungary in 1872 at Klosterneuburg, in the experimental vineyard of the viticultural school founded there in 1860, apparently introduced on American vines brought in for study. It spread through Lower Austria, Hungary and the Balkans over the next two decades, devastating Tokaj in the 1880s. Klosterneuburg's school, still Austria's main wine research institute, later played a central role in breeding new varieties such as Zweigelt.

events.title: Phylloxera spreads across the world
events.text: After France, phylloxera reached the Douro and Austria in the early 1870s, Germany and Switzerland by the mid-1870s, Victoria in Australia in 1877, Spain (Málaga, 1878) and Italy (1879), South Africa in 1886, Champagne in 1890 and Rioja in 1901. As French production collapsed, merchants bought wine from Rioja and Algeria, which boomed until phylloxera arrived there too. Only a few places escaped: Chile, much of South Australia, Cyprus, Santorini, Colares' sand dunes and parts of Washington State, where ungrafted vines still grow.
events.place: Europe and the wider wine world

events.title: Missouri Norton wins in Vienna
events.text: German immigrants in Hermann, Missouri, built a thriving wine industry on native grapes such as Norton and Catawba. A Missouri Norton won a medal at the 1873 Vienna World's Fair, and by the 1880s Missouri was among the leading wine states. Stone Hill Winery, founded in 1847, became one of the largest wineries in the country. Prohibition wiped it out, and its cellars were used to grow mushrooms until the winery was revived in 1965.

events.title: Phylloxera in California, twice
events.text: Phylloxera was found in Sonoma in 1873 and destroyed thousands of acres in the following decades. Replanting used the rootstock AxR1, a vinifera-rupestris cross recommended by UC Davis. In the 1980s a new biotype, phylloxera biotype B, attacked AxR1 vineyards in Napa and Sonoma, forcing growers to replant a large share of Napa and Sonoma's vineyards in the 1990s at a cost estimated in the billions of dollars, usually with denser plantings and better clones.

events.title: Phylloxera in Germany
events.text: Phylloxera was found in 1874 near Bonn, at the Annaberg estate. Germany responded with the Reblausgesetz (Phylloxera Act) of 1875, ordering infected vineyards destroyed and soil disinfected, and banning imports of vine material. The aggressive policy slowed the spread, and parts of the Mosel survived with own-rooted vines for decades. Ungrafted Riesling vines more than 100 years old still grow on the Mosel's slate slopes.

events.title: Phylloxera reaches Switzerland
events.text: The aphid was found at Pregny near Geneva in the early 1870s (sources give 1871 or 1874), probably arriving on vines from nurseries. Switzerland reacted with strict quarantine laws, and cantons such as the Valais, isolated in their Alpine valley, held it off for decades. Its slow spread helped preserve old indigenous varieties such as Petite Arvine, Humagne and Cornalin, some of which survived on their own roots into the 20th century.

events.title: Italian immigrants plant the Serra Gaúcha
events.text: From 1875, immigrants from the Veneto, Trentino and Lombardy settled the highlands of Rio Grande do Sul in southern Brazil, around what are now Bento Gonçalves, Caxias do Sul and Garibaldi. They planted vines, mostly American Isabella, which resisted the humid climate. The Serra Gaúcha remains the heart of Brazilian wine. In 2012 the Vale dos Vinhedos became Brazil's first Denomination of Origin, notable for its Merlot and traditional-method sparkling wines.
events.place: Bento Gonçalves, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil

events.title: Munson and Jaeger send rootstocks to France
events.text: Hermann Jaeger of Neosho, Missouri, and Thomas Volney Munson of Denison, Texas, studied wild American grape species and supplied millions of resistant cuttings, notably of Vitis berlandieri, riparia and rupestris, to French growers. In 1888 both received the French Legion of Honour. Munson's experimental vineyard became the T. V. Munson Viticulture Center in Denison. Their native species formed the basis of rootstocks such as 41B and 110 Richter, still used across the world.

events.title: Japan's first wine company
events.text: In 1877 two young men from Yamanashi, Masanari Takano and Ryuken Tsuchiya, were sent to Troyes in France to learn winemaking, returning in 1879 to work at the Dainihon Yamanashi Budoshu Company, Japan's first wine company, founded in Katsunuma. Using the local Koshu grape, grown in Yamanashi for centuries, they began a modern industry. Japan's wines remained mostly sweet until the late 20th century, and Koshu was registered with the OIV in 2010.

events.title: Phylloxera reaches Victoria
events.text: Phylloxera entered Australia undetected around 1875 and was confirmed at Geelong, Victoria, in 1877. The government paid growers to uproot vineyards, which ended Geelong's once-thriving industry, and the pest spread to Bendigo and Rutherglen. South Australia passed a Phylloxera Act in 1899 and enforced strict quarantine, keeping it out. As a result, the Barossa has some of the oldest ungrafted vines in the world, including Shiraz planted in the 1840s.

sources.title: Vinehealth Australia: 125 years of protecting vineyards

events.title: Phylloxera reaches Spain
events.text: Phylloxera was found in Málaga in 1877 to 1878 and in Catalonia (Girona) soon afterwards. Málaga's famous sweet wine industry was devastated, and its vineyard area never recovered. Spain had benefited from France's crisis, selling vast quantities of wine to French merchants, but the plague eventually reached Jerez (1894) and Rioja (1901). The Canary Islands and parts of La Mancha's sandy soils escaped.

events.title: Phylloxera reaches Italy
events.text: Phylloxera was first identified in Italy in 1879 at Valmadrera near Lecco in Lombardy, and in Sicily soon after. It spread slowly through the peninsula over the next 50 years, and Italian replanting was still under way in the 1930s. Some areas escaped because of sandy or volcanic soils, including parts of Etna, Campania and Sardinia, where ungrafted vines are still found. The slow pace allowed Italy to profit from French shortages for a time.

events.title: French Algeria becomes a wine giant
events.text: As phylloxera destroyed French vineyards, settlers in French Algeria planted vines on a vast scale. By the 1930s Algeria had several hundred thousand hectares of vines and was the world's largest wine exporter, shipping dark, high-alcohol reds to blend with lighter Midi wines. Algerian imports fuelled the overproduction that caused the 1907 Languedoc revolt. After independence in 1962 and the loss of the French market, most vineyards were uprooted, and Algeria's wine industry shrank to a fraction of its size.

events.title: Baron Edmond de Rothschild plants Israel's vineyards
events.text: Baron Edmond de Rothschild, owner of Château Lafite, funded Jewish agricultural colonies in Ottoman Palestine, including vineyards and wineries at Rishon LeZion (1890) and Zichron Ya'akov (1892). These became the Carmel winery, for decades the dominant producer in Israel. Modern Israeli fine wine began in the 1980s, when the Golan Heights Winery planted cooler, high-altitude vineyards and brought in Californian winemaking expertise. Today the country has hundreds of wineries, many kosher.

events.title: Millardet invents Bordeaux mixture
events.text: Downy mildew, another American import, reached France in 1878. Pierre-Marie-Alexis Millardet, a botany professor at Bordeaux, noticed in 1882 that Médoc vines near the road, which growers had sprayed with a blue mix of copper sulphate and lime to deter grape thieves, were free of the disease. In 1885 he published the formula of 'bouillie bordelaise'. Bordeaux mixture became the world's first widely used fungicide and is still allowed in organic viticulture.

events.title: Phylloxera reaches the Cape
events.text: Phylloxera reached the Cape in the 1880s (sources give 1880 or 1886), first found at Mowbray near Cape Town, and spread through Constantia, Stellenbosch and Paarl. Many farmers went bankrupt, and replanting with high-yielding varieties on American rootstocks led to overproduction by the early 1900s. That crisis led to the founding in 1918 of the KWV cooperative, which controlled the industry for most of the 20th century.

events.title: Viala's American mission
events.text: The French government sent Pierre Viala, a young professor at the Montpellier school of agriculture, to the United States to find rootstocks that could tolerate the chalky, high-limestone soils of Cognac and Champagne, where early American rootstocks failed with lime-induced chlorosis. With Munson's help, he identified Vitis berlandieri from the limestone hills of Texas. Crosses of berlandieri with riparia and rupestris made it possible to replant the great limestone regions of France.

events.title: Grafting rebuilds European viticulture
events.text: After years of failed remedies, including flooding vineyards and injecting carbon disulphide, French growers accepted grafting vinifera onto American rootstocks. Nurseries mass-produced bench grafts, and by about 1900 most of the French vineyard had been replanted. The reconstruction changed European wine: some regions shrank permanently, others switched varieties, and the vineyard moved from mixed field plantings to rows suited to ploughs. Hybrid direct producers such as Noah and Jacquez were also planted until they were banned in 1935.

events.title: Phylloxera reaches Champagne
events.text: Champagne was one of the last French regions to be hit, with the first outbreak found in 1890. The vineyards were replanted on American rootstocks over the following decades, a slow and costly process that ruined many growers and contributed to the anger behind the 1911 riots. Bollinger still farms tiny ungrafted parcels of Pinot Noir in Aÿ for its Vieilles Vignes Françaises cuvée, a rare survival of pre-phylloxera Champagne.

events.title: Changyu, China's first modern winery
events.text: Zhang Bishi, a wealthy overseas Chinese merchant, founded the Changyu Pioneer Wine Company in Yantai, Shandong, in 1892 with an imperial licence. He imported more than a hundred European varieties, including the vine later known as Cabernet Gernischt (identified by DNA as Carmenère), and dug large underground cellars. Changyu won gold medals at the 1915 Panama-Pacific Exposition in San Francisco and remains one of China's largest wine companies.

events.title: Prince Golitsyn and Massandra
events.text: Prince Lev Golitsyn, a pioneer of Russian sparkling and fortified wines, was appointed chief winemaker to the Tsar's estates in Crimea in 1891, building the Massandra winery near Yalta between 1894 and 1897 and its tunnels cut into the hillside. He also founded the sparkling wine estate at Novy Svet. Massandra's collection of about a million bottles includes sweet wines from the 18th century. Abrau-Dyurso near Novorossiysk, created in 1870, made Russia's imperial sparkling wine.

events.title: Phylloxera reaches Rioja
events.text: Phylloxera was confirmed in Rioja in 1901, near Sajazarra, ending the boom created by French buyers. The region had prepared: a viticultural station at Haro, opened in 1892, had studied American rootstocks, and replanting went faster than elsewhere. The Haro station's influence and the arrival of French techniques shaped the classic Rioja style of long ageing in American oak, and the Rioja Consejo Regulador was set up in 1925.

events.title: France's anti-fraud law
events.text: With phylloxera-era fraud rampant, from wine made of raisins and sugar to cheap Algerian blends sold under famous names, France passed a law against fraud in the sale of goods, followed by a 1908 decree enabling the delimitation of wine regions. Bordeaux, Champagne, Cognac and Armagnac were delimited in the following years. The approach, protecting a geographical name, led to the 1919 appellation of origin law and finally to the 1935 AOC system.

events.title: The revolt of the Midi winegrowers
events.text: Overproduction, cheap Algerian imports and sugared 'fake wine' sent prices crashing in the Languedoc. Marcelin Albert, a café owner from Argeliers, led a movement that brought hundreds of thousands of people into the streets: a rally in Montpellier on 9 June 1907 is often put at more than 500,000 people. Mayors resigned en masse, troops opened fire in Narbonne, killing several people, and the 17th Infantry Regiment mutinied at Béziers rather than fire on protesters. A law of 29 June 1907 required declarations of harvests and restricted sugar.

events.title: The Champagne riots
events.text: Champagne growers in the Marne, ruined by poor harvests and phylloxera, rioted against houses buying cheap grapes from outside the region, including the Loire and the Aube. In April 1911 rioters in Aÿ and Épernay sacked cellars and burned buildings, and thousands of troops were sent to occupy the region. Meanwhile growers in the Aube protested their exclusion from the delimited zone of 1908. The crisis led to the eventual inclusion of the Aube in 1927 and shaped Champagne's strict controls on grape origins.

events.title: South Africa's KWV is founded
events.text: To end a crisis of overproduction after phylloxera replanting, Cape growers formed the Koöperatieve Wijnbouwers Vereniging (KWV) in Paarl in 1918. Backed by law from 1924, it fixed minimum prices and production quotas and controlled exports for most of the century, favouring brandy and fortified wine. The system and apartheid-era sanctions isolated South African wine until the 1990s; the KWV became a private company in 1997, and the industry opened up quickly.

events.title: Prohibition in the United States
events.text: The 18th Amendment and the Volstead Act banned the production and sale of alcoholic drinks. Most American wineries closed or switched to grape juice and concentrates, but a loophole allowed households to make 200 gallons of 'fruit juice' a year, and sacramental wine remained legal. Growers shipped thick-skinned grapes such as Alicante Bouschet east, and grape acreage in California actually expanded. When repeal came in 1933, the industry had lost skills, and sweet fortified wines dominated for decades.

events.title: Châteauneuf-du-Pape writes its own rules
events.text: Baron Pierre Le Roy de Boiseaumarié, a lawyer and First World War pilot who had married into Château Fortia, persuaded Châteauneuf-du-Pape's growers to adopt strict rules: a delimited zone based on soils where lavender and thyme grew, permitted grape varieties, minimum alcohol, and a triage that discarded a share of the harvest. Recognised by a court in 1929 and by decree in 1933, the rules became the model for the national AOC system he co-founded in 1935.

events.title: Steiner lectures on biodynamic agriculture
events.text: At Koberwitz (now Kobierzyce, Poland), the Austrian philosopher Rudolf Steiner gave eight lectures to farmers that became the basis of biodynamic farming: farms as self-sustaining organisms, compost preparations, and work timed to lunar and cosmic rhythms. It reached wine decades later, when Nicolas Joly of the Coulée de Serrant began converting in 1980. Domaine Leroy, Leflaive, Zind-Humbrecht and many others followed, and the Demeter and Biodyvin certifications now cover hundreds of estates.

events.title: Perold creates Pinotage
events.text: Abraham Izak Perold, the first professor of viticulture at Stellenbosch University, crossed Pinot Noir with Cinsault (then known locally as Hermitage) at the Welgevallen experimental farm. He planted four seeds in his garden and left for a job at the KWV, and the seedlings were saved by a colleague when the garden was being cleared. Pinotage was released commercially in the 1940s and became South Africa's signature grape. The KWV cooperative, founded in 1918, controlled the industry for most of the century.

events.title: France creates the AOC system
events.text: A decree-law created the Comité National des Appellations d'Origine, which became the INAO, empowered to define appellations by geography, grape varieties, yields, minimum alcohol and production methods. Senator Joseph Capus and Baron Le Roy were its architects. The first AOCs, in 1936, included Arbois, Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Cassis, Tavel and Monbazillac. The AOC model, combining place and rules, inspired Italy's DOC (1963), Spain's DO system and the EU's protected designations of origin.

sources.title: Institut national de l'origine et de la qualité

events.title: France bans six American direct producers
events.text: The same year as the AOC law, France banned the planting of six American direct-producer varieties: Noah, Othello, Isabelle (Isabella), Jacquez, Clinton and Herbemont, citing poor quality and claims of high methanol. Many of these had been planted after phylloxera because they needed no grafting or spraying. The ban, later reflected in EU law, pushed hybrids into marginal use, though they survived in places such as Austria's Uhudler, Italy's Fragolino and the vineyards of Brazil and Moldova.

events.title: Dom Pérignon, the first prestige cuvée
events.text: Moët & Chandon released the 1921 vintage of Dom Pérignon in 1936, the first 'prestige cuvée' Champagne, in a replica 18th-century bottle. Its success during the Depression showed that luxury Champagne could be sold on a story and a name. Other houses followed with Louis Roederer's Cristal, created for Tsar Alexander II and sold commercially from 1945, Taittinger Comtes de Champagne and Krug's Grande Cuvée, creating the top tier of the modern Champagne market.

events.title: Burgundy's grand crus are named
events.text: Following the 1935 law, the INAO created Burgundy's appellations between 1936 and 1937, including the grand crus of the Côte d'Or such as Chambertin, Musigny, Romanée-Conti, La Tâche, Corton and Montrachet. The ranking drew on the 1861 classification by Jules Lavalle and the Beaune committee, which had graded vineyards as têtes de cuvée and premières cuvées. Burgundy's pyramid of regional, village, premier cru and grand cru appellations dates from this period, and the premier crus were added in the 1940s.

events.title: Wine under the German occupation
events.text: After France fell in 1940, Germany appointed 'Weinführer', wine merchants charged with buying French wine for the Reich, such as Otto Klaebisch in Champagne and Heinz Bömers in Bordeaux. Producers hid their best bottles behind false walls, and many cellars sheltered Resistance fighters and weapons. Robert-Jean de Vogüé of Moët & Chandon, who coordinated Champagne's relations with the occupiers, was arrested and sent to a concentration camp but survived.

events.title: Max Schubert makes the first Grange
events.text: After visiting Bordeaux in 1950, Penfolds chief winemaker Max Schubert set out to make an Australian red that could age like a first growth. His experimental 1951 Grange Hermitage used Shiraz, fermented in a way to extract colour and tannin, and finished in new American oak. Penfolds management disliked it and ordered production stopped in 1957, but Schubert kept making it in secret. Later vintages won acclaim, and Grange became Australia's most famous wine and a heritage icon.

events.title: England's first modern vineyard
events.text: Major-General Sir Guy Salisbury-Jones planted Seyval Blanc and other cold-tolerant varieties at Hambledon in Hampshire, the first commercial vineyard in England since the Middle Ages. English wine remained a curiosity for decades, but chalk soils similar to Champagne's and warming summers later made English sparkling wine viable. Nyetimber in West Sussex, planted in 1988 with Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier, showed what was possible when its 1992 sparkling won international awards.

events.title: Moldova's underground wine cities
events.text: Limestone mines under the villages of Cricova and Mileștii Mici near Chișinău were turned into cellars in the 1950s and 1960s. Cricova's galleries run for more than 100 kilometres, with streets named after wines, and Mileștii Mici's tunnels hold what Guinness World Records recognised in 2005 as the world's largest wine collection, about 1.5 million bottles. Moldova was the Soviet Union's leading wine supplier, and Russian embargoes in 2006 and 2013 forced it to turn toward the EU.

events.title: Italy's DOC law
events.text: Italy's Presidential Decree 930 of 1963 created the Denominazione di Origine Controllata system, modelled on the French AOC. The first DOC, Vernaccia di San Gimignano, came in 1966, and the top category, DOCG, was first awarded to Brunello di Montalcino, Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, Barolo and Barbaresco in 1980. The system's rigid rules, which required white grapes in Chianti, pushed innovators to bottle outside it as vino da tavola, leading to the Super Tuscans.

events.title: Robert Mondavi opens his winery in Oakville
events.text: Robert Mondavi left the family's Charles Krug winery after a dispute with his brother and built a new winery in Oakville, the first major new winery in Napa since Prohibition. Its mission-style arch became an icon. Mondavi promoted varietal labelling, cold fermentation, French oak barrels and wine as part of gracious living. In 1979 he partnered with Baron Philippe de Rothschild to create Opus One, a symbol of Napa's arrival among the great wine regions.

events.title: Germany's 1971 wine law
events.text: West Germany's new wine law classified quality wine by the sugar content of grapes at harvest (the Prädikat ladder from Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese) rather than by vineyard. It also merged roughly 30,000 named vineyard sites into about 2,600 Einzellagen and created Grosslagen, broad collective sites whose names sounded like single vineyards. The law has been criticised for decades for blurring the distinction between great and ordinary sites. It was reformed in 2021 toward an origin-based pyramid.

events.title: The Super Tuscans
events.text: Marchese Mario Incisa della Rocchetta had made a Cabernet-based wine at Bolgheri for family use since the 1940s; Sassicaia's 1968 vintage, released in 1971, was its commercial debut. The same year Piero Antinori made the first Tignanello, a Sangiovese aged in French barriques that later took in Cabernet. Both were classified as humble vino da tavola because they broke DOC rules. Their success created the 'Super Tuscan' category, and Sassicaia, a subzone of the new Bolgheri DOC from 1994, became Italy's only single-estate DOC, Bolgheri Sassicaia, in 2013.

events.title: Mouton Rothschild becomes a first growth
events.text: After a five-decade campaign, Baron Philippe de Rothschild won the only change to the 1855 classification's top tier: Château Mouton Rothschild was promoted from second to first growth by decree of Jacques Chirac, then minister of agriculture. The estate's motto changed from 'First I cannot be, second I do not deign to be, Mouton I am' to 'First I am, second I was, Mouton does not change'. Since 1945 Mouton has commissioned an artist for each vintage's label; the 1973 label is by Picasso.

events.title: Europe's wine lake and vine-pull schemes
events.text: Overproduction in the European Economic Community, much of it from high-yielding southern vineyards, created a 'wine lake' disposed of by subsidised crisis distillation. The EEC restricted new plantings from 1976 and, from 1988, paid growers to grub up vines permanently. Hundreds of thousands of hectares were removed in the following decades, especially in the Languedoc, Italy and Spain. The policy set the pattern for later grubbing-up schemes, including those of 2008 to 2011 and the 2020s.

events.title: The Judgment of Paris
events.text: Steven Spurrier, an English wine merchant in Paris, and Patricia Gallagher organised a blind tasting of California and French wines judged by nine French experts at the InterContinental hotel. Chateau Montelena's 1973 Chardonnay and Stag's Leap Wine Cellars' 1973 Cabernet Sauvignon won. George Taber, the only journalist present, reported it in Time magazine. The result shocked the wine world, boosted Napa's reputation and showed that great wine could come from outside Europe.

events.title: Augusta becomes the first AVA
events.text: Regulations adopted in 1978 by the federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms created American Viticultural Areas, defined by geography rather than grape variety or method. The first, approved on 20 June 1980, was Augusta, Missouri, recognising its 19th-century German winemaking heritage, eight months before Napa Valley. An AVA requires 85 percent of grapes from the area. There were more than 270 AVAs by 2024, approved by the TTB since 2003.

events.title: Robert Parker and the 100-point scale
events.text: Robert Parker, a lawyer from Maryland who began publishing The Wine Advocate in 1978 with a 100-point scoring system, declared the 1982 Bordeaux vintage outstanding when many established critics were cautious. He was proved right, and his influence grew enormously. For two decades his scores moved prices and styles worldwide; critics accused him of encouraging riper, oakier wines. The 100-point scale became the global standard for wine criticism.

events.title: Austria's antifreeze scandal
events.text: Investigators found that some Austrian producers and merchants, mostly in Burgenland, had added diethylene glycol, a sweet compound used in some antifreeze, to make thin wines taste richer and sweeter, imitating late-harvest Prädikat wines. Austrian wine exports collapsed. The government responded with one of the strictest wine laws in the world in August 1985, with controls on volumes, labels and sweetness, and a new generation turned to dry, quality-focused wine.

events.title: Cloudy Bay launches Marlborough Sauvignon
events.text: Montana had planted Marlborough's first commercial vineyard in 1973 and released a Sauvignon Blanc in 1980. In 1985 David Hohnen of Cape Mentelle in Western Australia launched Cloudy Bay, whose pungent, gooseberry-and-passion fruit Sauvignon Blanc, with its misty mountain label, became an international cult wine. Marlborough grew from a sheep-farming district to New Zealand's largest wine region, and Sauvignon Blanc now accounts for most of the country's wine exports.

events.title: Gorbachev's anti-alcohol campaign
events.text: Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev launched a campaign against alcoholism in May 1985, raising prices, limiting sales and ordering vineyards uprooted. Across the USSR about a third of vineyards were destroyed, with heavy losses in Moldova, Ukraine, Crimea, Georgia and southern Russia; Massandra and Abrau-Dyurso lost famous plots. The campaign cut state revenue and was abandoned by 1988, but it set back the wine industries of the region for decades.

events.title: Italy's methanol scandal
events.text: Cheap Barbera wine from a producer in Narzole, Piedmont, had been adulterated with methanol to raise its alcohol content. Twenty-three people died and many others were blinded. Italian wine exports collapsed, and the scandal forced a crackdown on bulk producers and stricter controls. Combined with the Austrian scandal of 1985, it pushed European wine regulation toward traceability and quality, and helped launch a generation of Italian producers focused on quality.

events.title: The New World export boom
events.text: In the 1990s Australia, Chile, Argentina, South Africa and New Zealand turned their industries toward export, offering fruit-forward varietal wines at low prices and with simple labels. Australia's exports grew more than tenfold during the decade, and brands such as Jacob's Creek and, from 2001, Yellow Tail became bestsellers in Britain and the US. The end of apartheid opened South Africa's markets in 1994, and Chile's democratic transition encouraged foreign investment, from Miguel Torres to the Rothschilds.

events.title: Inniskillin's icewine wins in Bordeaux
events.text: Donald Ziraldo and Karl Kaiser founded Inniskillin at Niagara-on-the-Lake in 1975, receiving Ontario's first new winery licence since Prohibition. In 1991 their 1989 Vidal Icewine won the Grand Prix d'Honneur at Vinexpo in Bordeaux, putting Canadian wine on the map. Ontario's VQA system began in 1988 and became law in 1999. Canada is now the world's leading icewine producer, making it from grapes frozen on the vine at minus 8 degrees Celsius or colder.

events.title: Carmenère rediscovered in Chile
events.text: Visiting Chile, the French ampelographer Jean-Michel Boursiquot recognised that many vines grown as Merlot were in fact Carmenère, an old Bordeaux variety thought almost extinct. Chile's agriculture ministry officially recognised the grape in 1998. It became Chile's signature red, and the story shows how Chile's pre-phylloxera vineyards had preserved 19th-century Bordeaux plant material that disappeared in France.

events.title: DNA reveals grape parents
events.text: John Bowers and Carole Meredith at UC Davis used microsatellite DNA markers to show in 1997 that Cabernet Sauvignon is a cross of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc. In 1999, with French colleagues, they showed that Chardonnay, Gamay, Aligoté, Melon and 12 other varieties are siblings born of Pinot and the peasant grape Gouais Blanc. These studies launched a revolution in grape genealogy that has since mapped the parents of hundreds of varieties.

events.title: Sula Vineyards and Indian wine
events.text: Rajeev Samant, a Stanford-educated engineer who had worked in Silicon Valley, planted vines on his family's land near Nashik in Maharashtra and released Sula's first wines in 2000. Nashik became India's wine capital, with dozens of wineries on the Deccan plateau at about 600 metres, where vines are pruned to fruit in the dry winter rather than the monsoon. Sula listed on the Indian stock exchange in 2022. Indian wine remains small but fast-growing.

events.title: Clare Valley and New Zealand adopt screwcaps
events.text: Frustrated by cork taint (TCA) and random oxidation, 13 Clare Valley Riesling producers bottled their 2000 vintage under screwcaps, and in 2001 New Zealand producers formed the New Zealand Screwcap Wine Seal Initiative. Within a decade most Australian and New Zealand wine, including premium reds, was screwcapped. The move forced cork producers to improve quality and opened a debate on how closures affect ageing that continues today.

events.title: Ningxia and China's wine boom
events.text: China's wine consumption grew rapidly in the 2000s, and the government designated the eastern foothills of the Helan Mountains in Ningxia as a protected origin in 2003. In 2011 Jia Bei Lan 2009 from Helan Qingxue won the top international trophy for a Bordeaux varietal red at the Decanter World Wine Awards, and the region launched its own classification of châteaux in 2013. Hong Kong's abolition of wine duty in 2008 made it a hub of the fine wine trade. China briefly became the largest red wine market in the world.

events.title: EU wine reform creates PDO and PGI
events.text: The EU wine reform of 2008, applied from August 2009, replaced the old split between 'quality wine produced in a specified region' and table wine with two categories: Protected Designation of Origin (PDO) and Protected Geographical Indication (PGI), aligning wine with other agricultural products. Member states kept their own terms (AOC, DOC, DO, Qualitätswein), but registration moved to the EU's eAmbrosia database. The reform also funded a grubbing-up scheme of about 175,000 hectares from 2008 to 2011.

events.title: Rudy Kurniawan arrested
events.text: The FBI arrested Rudy Kurniawan, a collector who had sold millions of dollars of rare Burgundy and Bordeaux at auction, at his home in Arcadia, California, finding labels, corks and recipes for faking old wines. Laurent Ponsot of Domaine Ponsot had exposed him by pulling a 2008 auction of 'Clos Saint-Denis' vintages from before his domaine made the wine. Kurniawan was convicted in 2013 and sentenced to ten years. The case transformed authentication in the fine-wine trade.

events.title: UNESCO recognises qvevri winemaking
events.text: UNESCO inscribed the 'ancient Georgian traditional qvevri wine-making method' on its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. In qvevri winemaking, grapes, often with skins, stems and seeds, ferment and age in large egg-shaped clay vessels buried in the ground, sealed for months. The recognition boosted international interest in Georgia and in amber or orange wines, and inspired producers from Friuli to Australia to use qvevri and amphorae.

events.title: Champagne houses buy into England
events.text: Warming summers and chalk soils like Champagne's drew French investors across the Channel. Taittinger bought farmland at Chilham near Canterbury in 2014, announced its Domaine Evremond project in 2015, planted from 2017 and released its first wine in 2025. Pommery released an English sparkling with Hattingley Valley in 2017 and bought land in Hampshire. English vineyard area roughly tripled between 2010 and the mid-2020s, and English sparkling wine gained its own protected designations.

events.title: Burgundy's climats and Champagne join UNESCO
events.text: On the same day, UNESCO inscribed the Climats of Burgundy (1,247 named vineyard plots of the Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune) and the Champagne Hillsides, Houses and Cellars on the World Heritage List. They joined earlier wine landscapes such as Saint-Émilion (1999), the Alto Douro (2001), Tokaj (2002), Pico in the Azores (2004) and Lavaux (2007). The listings recognised vineyard landscapes as cultural achievements shaped by centuries of human work.

events.title: Bordeaux approves climate-change grapes
events.text: The INAO approved six new varieties for Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur, the first change to the permitted grape list in decades: reds Arinarnoa, Castets, Marselan and Touriga Nacional, and whites Alvarinho and Liliorila. They may make up to 5 percent of vineyard area and 10 percent of a blend. The move responds to hotter summers that push Merlot to high alcohol, and it signalled a wider rethinking of appellation rules in the face of climate change.

events.title: The great April frost
events.text: After an unusually warm March pushed vines into early bud, temperatures fell as low as minus 6 degrees Celsius across France on three nights in early April. Growers lit thousands of candles and braziers in the vineyards, creating images seen around the world, and helicopters stirred the air. Losses were severe from Burgundy and Chablis to the Rhône, Loire and Bordeaux, and in northern Italy. The French government declared an agricultural disaster, and the 2021 French harvest was one of the smallest in decades.

events.title: Germany reforms its wine law
events.text: Germany amended its wine law in 2021 to move from a ripeness-based system toward an origin-based pyramid, similar to France's: Gutswein (estate), Ortswein (village), Erste Lage and Grosse Lage at the top, with smaller origins having stricter rules. Grosslagen names must be shown more clearly as regional, and the changes are being phased in over the 2020s. The reform formalised ideas the VDP growers' association had promoted since the early 2000s.

events.title: Bordeaux pays growers to pull up vines
events.text: Falling demand for red Bordeaux, especially in China and France, left many growers unable to sell their wine. In 2023 the French state and the Bordeaux wine council (CIVB) financed a plan to grub up about 8,000 hectares, half for sanitary reasons and half to switch land to other crops, paying 6,000 euros per hectare. More than 1,200 applications were filed. The plan, alongside crisis distillation, marked a shrinking of the world's most famous wine region.

events.title: Science paper rewrites the domestication story
events.text: A team of 89 researchers led by Yang Dong of Yunnan Agricultural University and Wei Chen published in Science the largest genetic study of grapevines yet, based on 3,525 cultivated and wild samples. They concluded that grapes were domesticated about 11,000 years ago, at the same time as cereals, in two centres, the South Caucasus and western Asia, and that wine grapes in Western Europe owe much of their ancestry to crossing with local wild vines along the way.

events.title: China lifts its tariffs on Australian wine
events.text: In 2020, amid diplomatic tensions, China imposed anti-dumping and countervailing duties of up to 218 percent on Australian wine, wiping out a market worth about 1.2 billion Australian dollars a year, then Australia's largest. After a review, China's commerce ministry removed the duties from 29 March 2024. Shipments resumed quickly, but the episode had left Australia with a large surplus, prompting vineyard removals in the Riverland and Riverina.

events.title: World wine output falls to a 60-year low
events.text: Frost, drought, heavy rain and mildew cut harvests across both hemispheres in 2023 and 2024. The OIV reported that world wine production in 2024 was the lowest since 1961, and consumption also fell to its lowest level in decades, as younger drinkers drank less and health warnings increased. OIV's first estimate for 2025, released in November 2025, put production at about 232 million hectolitres, slightly up on 2024 but 7 percent below the five-year average.

events.title: US tariffs hit wine imports
events.text: In March 2025 the US threatened 200 percent tariffs on European wine, and in April imposed a 10 percent tariff on most imports. In August the EU-US framework agreement set a 15 percent tariff on most EU goods, with no exemption for wine or spirits despite EU lobbying. Canada's provinces, starting with Ontario's LCBO on 4 March 2025, removed American wine and spirits from their shelves in retaliation. Importers, distributors and restaurants on both sides of the Atlantic reported falling sales.

events.title: Champagne cuts yields again
events.text: Faced with falling shipments and large stocks, Champagne's interprofession set the 2026 commercial yield at one of the lowest levels of the century, a fourth consecutive reduction, and aimed to cap production at about 250 million bottles. The decision reflected weaker global demand for sparkling wine after the post-pandemic boom and the effect of tariffs. Lower yields also help growers keep prices stable, but they cut income for the region's 16,000 growers.

events.title: The EU's wine package
events.text: The European Parliament approved, by 625 votes to 15, a package of measures agreed with member states in December 2025 to support a sector facing falling consumption, tariffs and climate stress. It allows EU funds to pay for grubbing up vines, raises support for wine tourism and promotion abroad, adds crisis aid after extreme weather, and sets labelling terms for low-alcohol wine: 'alcohol-free' with 0.0 percent for wine at or below 0.05 percent alcohol, and 'alcohol reduced' for wines at least 30 percent below their category's normal strength.

events.title: US Supreme Court strikes down emergency tariffs
events.text: In Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not authorise the sweeping tariffs imposed in 2025, including those on wine. The administration immediately imposed temporary tariffs of up to 15 percent under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, valid for 150 days, and opened country-specific investigations. Importers began seeking refunds, and the uncertainty continued to weigh on transatlantic and Canadian wine trade through 2026.
